Trying to Conceive

Preparing for pregnancy: practical steps before you start trying

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Preparing for pregnancy is something you can begin over the weeks or months before conception. It is not a ritual to complete immediately before sex, and it cannot guarantee a particular outcome. A few well-chosen steps can help reduce avoidable risks and make it easier to get support when you need it.

Start folic acid before conception

For most people planning pregnancy, the usual recommendation is 400 micrograms of folic acid daily, starting at least a month before conception and continuing through early pregnancy. Many local guidelines specify the first 12 weeks, with a suitable prenatal supplement continuing as advised.

Check the label: 400 micrograms is 0.4 milligrams, not 1 milligram. Folate-rich foods remain useful, but they do not replace the recommended supplement. Folic acid reduces the chance of neural tube defects; it is not an intelligence booster or a fertility treatment.

Some people need a prescribed higher dose because of a previous affected pregnancy, certain medicines or medical conditions. The dose and eligibility differ by country. Ask before taking several tablets or combining supplements; taking metformin alone is not a universal reason to self-prescribe 5 milligrams.

Discuss other supplements according to your diet, health and local guidance. More is not automatically better, and some high-dose vitamins or herbal fertility products may be unsuitable.

Tell the clinician if you have coeliac disease, diabetes, take antiseizure medicines or metformin, or have had a pregnancy affected by a neural tube defect. These are reasons to review nutrition and medicines; they do not all mean the same folic-acid dose is appropriate. Hydrocephalus has several causes and is not automatically a neural tube defect.

Review health conditions and medicines

A preconception appointment is especially useful if you have a long-term condition, take regular medicines, have had pregnancy complications or need help with mental health or substance use. A partner’s health and medicines can also matter.

Bring a list of prescriptions, non-prescription products and supplements. Do not stop an essential treatment suddenly. The aim is to keep the condition well controlled while choosing a plan suited to pregnancy.

Ask whether cervical screening is due and whether STI testing or other checks are appropriate. Screening is not automatically repeated simply because you want to conceive, and no single test provides a complete guarantee of health.

Discuss relevant family history and the genetic carrier screening available to you. If you expect to use donor sperm, donor eggs or fertility treatment, the clinic can explain the preparation and testing that applies to that pathway.

Check vaccinations early

Review your vaccination record before trying. Some vaccines, including measles-mumps-rubella and chickenpox vaccines, are not given during pregnancy and may need to be arranged beforehand if you are not protected.

After an MMR dose, current US guidance advises avoiding pregnancy for 28 days. Follow the interval given for the exact vaccine you receive; a universal one-to-three-month delay is not appropriate for every vaccine.

Other vaccines may be recommended during pregnancy itself. For example, US guidance recommends Tdap in each pregnancy, regardless of a recent routine tetanus booster. Schedules and eligibility vary by country, so use your local pregnancy vaccination plan.

Include hepatitis B and routine tetanus vaccination in the record review. A routine booster schedule and the pertussis-containing vaccine advised during each pregnancy serve different purposes, so a recent tetanus dose does not automatically replace pregnancy vaccination.

Choose sustainable food and activity habits

Aim for a varied diet with vegetables, fruit, whole grains, protein sources and appropriate calcium-rich foods. Affordable options and culturally familiar meals can fit. There is no single fertility diet that guarantees conception.

Regular activity can support general health, sleep and wellbeing. Choose something manageable, such as walking, and adjust for medical advice or physical limitations. A daily exercise target should not be presented as a promise of a large fertility increase.

Both inadequate energy intake and some weight-related health problems can affect ovulation. Seek individual support if periods are irregular, weight is changing rapidly or eating is difficult. BMI is only one screening measure and does not capture every person’s health.

Avoid crash diets or delaying a needed fertility assessment indefinitely to reach an arbitrary number. Changes in weight do not guarantee that ovulation will return, and people in many body sizes have healthy pregnancies.

Practical food choices include aiming for at least five portions of fruit and vegetables a day, using proteins such as lean meat, poultry, eggs, fish, beans or lentils, and choosing milk, yoghurt, cheese or suitable calcium-fortified alternatives. Leafy greens, broccoli, Brussels sprouts, peas and oranges provide folate, but they do not replace the recommended folic-acid supplement.

Walking, cycling or an appropriate yoga session may fit an activity routine, with about 30 minutes a manageable example for some people and shorter sessions for others. A partner’s weight and metabolic health can also be relevant to fertility, but BMI alone cannot predict conception. Common adult BMI reference categories use 18.5–24.9 for the standard range; individual health assessment matters more than reaching a single number.

Reduce exposures and ask for help with substances

Avoid alcohol while trying to become pregnant because pregnancy may begin before a missed period. If stopping is difficult or you may be dependent, ask for medical support. A partner should also discuss heavy drinking or other substance use that may affect health and fertility.

Stopping smoking benefits health. Get support for tobacco, vaping or other nicotine use, and reduce secondhand smoke where possible. This is a shared household task rather than a burden for one person.

Keeping caffeine within the pregnancy recommendation of no more than 200 milligrams a day is a practical approach while trying. Count coffee, tea, energy drinks and other sources together; you do not necessarily have to stop caffeine completely.

If your work involves a reproductive hazard, ask occupational health or your clinician about the actual exposure and protective measures. Working with chemicals or radiation does not automatically mean you must leave your job. A specific risk assessment is more useful than a blanket instruction.

Smoking, including hookah or waterpipe tobacco, increases pregnancy risks such as growth problems, preterm birth and stillbirth. Stopping before pregnancy is useful, and stopping at any stage still matters. If reducing caffeine gradually is easier, do so while counting chocolate, soft drinks and caffeinated blends as well as tea and coffee.

Make space for support, finances and intimacy

Talk about practical matters such as time off, care costs, household work and whom you can ask for help. The purpose is to make needs visible, not to pass a financial or emotional readiness test.

Sleep, rest and enjoyable activities are worth protecting for your wellbeing. Ordinary worry is not proof that you are preventing conception, and being told to relax is not a substitute for fertility care.

If conceiving through intercourse, sex every two to three days across the cycle is a practical option. People who prefer tracking may choose intercourse every one to two days during the fertile window. You do not need a clinician to identify one perfect moment in every cycle.

There is no proven conception advantage from a special sexual position or from lying with your legs raised afterwards. If sex is painful, difficult or becoming stressful, ask for help rather than pushing through it.

The fertile window exists because sperm can remain capable of fertilisation for several days, whereas an egg has a much shorter usable period after ovulation. Regular intercourse or optional tracking can cover that window without a precise prediction for every cycle.

Know when to seek fertility advice

As a common clinical approach, assessment is offered after 12 months of trying when the person providing eggs is under 35, or after six months at 35 or older. Over 40, earlier discussion is appropriate. Local access pathways may differ.

Seek advice sooner for absent or very irregular periods, a known fertility condition, previous treatment that can affect fertility, or difficulty having intercourse. Both partners should be considered when relevant. Preparation supports health, but it does not replace evaluation when conception is taking longer than expected.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

CDC recommends 400 micrograms of folic acid daily before pregnancy for most people and separate clinician-directed regimens for higher-risk situations.

NHS and ASRM encourage health and medicine review, regular intercourse, sustainable habits and timely fertility assessment; no preparation checklist guarantees pregnancy.

How BeMama can help

Turn the fourteen preparation topics into a manageable appointment list covering supplements, medicines, vaccination, work exposures and practical support.

When to seek help

Review essential medicines and high-dose supplements with a clinician; do not stop treatment abruptly or delay indicated fertility care for a body-weight target.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Begin the recommended folic acid supplement before pregnancy.
  • Review medicines without stopping treatment on your own.
  • Check vaccinations and any screening that is actually due.
  • Choose manageable habits; perfection does not determine pregnancy success.
  • Get fertility advice according to age, history and how long you have been trying.

Frequently asked questions

Does everyone need 1 milligram of folic acid?

No. A common routine dose is 400 micrograms, or 0.4 milligrams. Higher-dose recommendations require individual advice.

Do we need to identify the exact day of ovulation?

No. Regular intercourse across the cycle can cover the fertile window. Tracking is optional unless a treatment plan requires it.

Should I stop my medication before trying?

Do not stop prescribed medicines without review. Your clinician can help balance treatment needs and pregnancy considerations.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
